strengths: The paper addresses a genuine gap: most implicit-bias analyses of steepest descent (including Fan et al., 2025, which is the closest prior work) assume full-batch gradients, while practical optimizers (SignSGD/Signum, Normalized-SGD, Muon) are mini-batch. The unified framework covering entry-wise and Schatten-p norms under standard random reshuffling (rather than fixed batch partitions as in Baek et al., 2025) is a valuable unification.

The main results are well-structured and interpretable: (i) a large-batch condition b > 4Rn/(γ+4R) for convergence without momentum, with an explicit batch-dependent margin gap γ−ρ; (ii) a batch–momentum trade-off where momentum removes the large-batch requirement; (iii) variance reduction recovering the exact full-batch max-margin solution for any batch size; (iv) a concrete negative result (Theorem 4.9) showing per-sample updates converge to a sample-averaged bias direction rather than the max-margin solution. The negative result is a nice contribution that clarifies the scope of the positive results.

There is real technical novelty in the proofs, notably Lemma C.12, which exploits the epoch-wise zero-sum structure of random reshuffling to bound accumulated momentum error, and Lemma C.15, which gives an explicit closed-form constant c2 = O(c1/(1−β)²) for the learning-rate Assumption 3.4. The removal of dimension dependence d from the rates of Fan et al. (2025) via a global ℓ1-norm argument on the gradient difference is a genuine tightening of the full-batch result.

The experiments (Figures 1–4, spanning ℓ2, ℓ∞, and spectral geometries, plus the per-sample validation in Appendix J) qualitatively match the theory: mini-batch breaks the full-batch bias, large momentum restores it, and variance reduction removes batch dependence. The per-sample experiment distinguishes convergence to the predicted bias direction W̄ from the max-margin solution.

The limitations section is honest and appropriate: restriction to linear classifiers on separable data, potentially conservative large-batch conditions, and the constructed-dataset nature of the batch-size-one analysis.
weaknesses: The parameter conditions behind the headline claims are quite restrictive, which the text underplays. The momentum condition ρ := γ − 2(1−β1)m(m²−1)R > 0 requires β1 ≳ 1 − γ/(2m³R) for large m — i.e., near-unity momentum for even moderate epoch sizes m = n/b — so the claimed 'small-batch convergence via momentum' holds only in a narrow regime. The VR results are exact but come with rates degraded by factors like m^{2+a}/(1−β1), making the exactness–speed trade-off potentially severe.

All rates are transient/asymptotic bounds on linear classifiers with polynomial learning rates ηt = ct^{-a}; the practically relevant constant-step-size regime, which is what Muon/Signum use in practice, is not covered. The contribution's connection to large-scale pretraining (motivated via Muon/LLM training in the introduction) is therefore somewhat indirect.

The experiments are small-scale, purely synthetic, and linear (n=200, d=5 in the main text), so they validate the theory on its own terms but do not probe whether the implicit-bias phenomena matter for the deep-network settings motivating the work.

Presentation has a number of distracting typos and inconsistencies: 'por any p ≥ 1' (Lemma C.1 proof), 'sequnece', 'Moementum' (Theorem E.4), 'perform deeper explorations' in the abstract, Lemma E.1's statement citing a constant '(e)' in the derivation, and inconsistent use of ρ vs. γ−4(n/b−1)R between the main text and Appendix D (Theorem D.4 vs. Corollary D.5 vs. Theorem 4.1). Lemma E.1 also claims the momentum analysis 'does not recover the no-momentum result' — the β1→0 singular behavior deserves clearer discussion since it makes the momentum and non-momentum theories appear disconnected.

Novelty is incremental relative to Fan et al. (2025): the full-batch max-margin result, proxy function G(W), and much of the technical machinery (Lemmas C.1–C.10) are imported from that work, with the stochastic noise control being the main new layer. The independent significance rests on how much value the stochastic extension and the negative result carry, which is substantial but not exceptional.

strengths: Unified framework: the paper casts SignSGD, Signum, Normalized-SGD, Spectral-SGD, and Muon (plus momentum and SVRG-style variance-reduced variants) as instances of one stochastic steepest-descent scheme under random reshuffling, which makes the batch-size/momentum analysis apply across several practically relevant optimizers.

Explicit, dimension-free margin convergence rates (Corollaries 4.2, 4.5, 4.7), including a genuine technical improvement over Fan et al. (2025) by removing the dimension-d dependence from the rate via a global l1-norm argument.

A clean qualitative message: variance reduction restores the exact full-batch norm-induced max-margin bias for any batch size, while momentum trades exactness for a batch-size relaxation; this is a coherent picture of when stochastic training aligns with full-batch implicit bias.

Honest limitations section identifying the linear/separable setting, potentially conservative large-batch condition, and the constructed nature of the batch-size-one example; extensive appendix with detailed proofs; experiments qualitatively track the theoretical trends (no momentum fails in mini-batch, large momentum or VR restores convergence).
weaknesses: The sufficient conditions underlying the main theorems appear incompatible with the paper's own experiments, leaving a large unacknowledged theory-practice gap. The large-batch condition rho = gamma - 4(m-1)R > 0 forces m < 1 + gamma/(4R), i.e., essentially full batch whenever gamma << R (typical when ||x_i||_1 = R is the natural scale). Worse, the momentum condition rho = gamma - 2(1-beta_1)m(m^2-1)R > 0 with the experimental setting (n=200, b=20 so m=10, beta_1=0.99) would require gamma > 19.8R, which is impossible since gamma = O(R). Yet Figures 1(d)/(f) show convergence in exactly this regime, so the 'batch-momentum trade-off' quantified by Theorem 4.3 does not explain the paper's own empirical results; the abstract's claim that 'momentum enables small-batch convergence' also obscures that the condition scales cubically in m.

The core novelty is incremental: the analysis is a stochastic extension of Fan et al. (2025)'s full-batch framework, and a substantial portion of the appendix (Lemmas C.1-C.10 and their proofs) restates Fan et al.'s lemmas. The genuine technical delta is the mini-batch noise and momentum-drift bookkeeping (Lemmas C.11-C.14), which is careful but bounded by worst-case arguments (e.g., Lemma C.11 bounds mini-batch noise by summing over the entire dataset with the larger coefficient), making the resulting conditions and rates likely very loose; no lower bounds or tightness discussion is provided.

The batch-size-one 'fundamentally different bias' result (Theorem 4.9) is established only on a specially constructed orthogonal scale-skewed dataset where per-sample update directions are constant matrices. This makes the epoch-level analysis nearly trivial (deterministic recurrence plus a convergent drift series) and does not establish that the departure from max-margin bias occurs for generic data; the implied claim that 'there may not exist a unified implicit bias theory' rests on this single contrived instance.

The empirical validation is confined to a tiny synthetic linear problem (n=200, d=5, T=20,000 iterations). No real datasets, nonlinear models, or actual Adam/Muon training are considered, so the practical relevance of the batch/momentum/VR trade-offs for the large-scale settings motivating the paper is untested. No code release is mentioned, which limits reproducibility of the figures.

Presentation quality is below the bar for a main-track theory paper: numerous typos and inconsistencies (e.g., 'perform deeper explorations', 'Moementum', 'similat', Lemma F.2 citing 'Assumptions 3.1, 3.2, and 3.2'), and the proof of Lemma C.5 loosely interchanges a max over A with a weighted sum without justification (the stated result is recoverable via the max-margin direction, but the written argument is not rigorous as given). These issues, while individually minor, collectively reduce confidence in the fine-grained rate statements.

strengths: Unified and well-motivated framework: the paper casts SignSGD, Signum, Normalized-SGD, Spectral-SGD, and Muon as instances of stochastic steepest descent under general entry-wise/Schatten-p norm geometries, and studies implicit bias for all of them simultaneously, which is a clean generalization of the full-batch analysis of Fan et al. (2025).

Meaningful conceptual contribution: the paper cleanly separates regimes — large batch without momentum yields only an approximate (batch-dependent) max-margin solution; momentum enables small-batch convergence via a batch-momentum tradeoff; variance reduction restores the exact full-batch bias at a rate cost; and batch-size-one updates can converge to a fundamentally different bias. This gives a coherent picture of when stochastic steepest descent aligns with full-batch behavior.

Technical improvements over prior work: the momentum analysis removes the dimension dependence in the rate of Fan et al. (2025) by exploiting a global l1-norm bound on gradient differences, and explicitly characterizes how beta_1 and m = n/b enter the convergence rate, which prior implicit-bias analyses (Zhang et al. 2024, Fan et al. 2025) did not capture.

Analysis is carried out under standard random reshuffling (sampling without replacement) rather than the fixed-batch cycling of Back et al. (2025), and provides finite-time rates, not just asymptotics — both are practical improvements.

Extensive appendix with detailed proofs (descent lemmas, epoch-wise zero-sum structure of reshuffling noise, explicit constants via Lemma C.15), and experiments across l2, l_infty, and spectral geometries that qualitatively match the theoretical predictions, including a dedicated validation of the batch-size-one result (Figure 2).

Honest limitations section correctly identifying that the analysis is restricted to linear classifiers on separable data, that the large-batch condition is conservative, and that the batch-size-one analysis is confined to a constructed dataset.
weaknesses: The main result without momentum (Theorem 4.1) only guarantees convergence to an approximate max-margin solution with persistent gap gamma - rho = 4(n/b - 1)R for any fixed b < n. The iterates do not converge to the true full-batch max-margin solution unless b approaches n, so the headline claim of 'recovering' the full-batch bias is weaker than it may first appear, and the required batch size b > 4Rn/(gamma + 4R) can be a substantial fraction of n for small margins.

A noticeable disconnect between the momentum and no-momentum analyses: Remark 4.4 concedes that the momentum result does not recover the no-momentum case at beta_1 = 0, and the momentum machinery breaks down in the degenerate case. This leaves the theory as two separate regimes rather than a unified characterization, and the momentum effective-margin condition rho = gamma - 2(1-beta_1)m(m^2-1)R > 0 becomes prohibitive when m is large unless beta_1 is very close to 1.

Scope of the theory is limited to linear multi-class classifiers on linearly separable data, while the motivating applications (Muon, Signum for LLM pretraining) involve deep networks; the paper does not offer any evidence or argument for transfer to non-homogeneous or nonlinear settings.

Empirical validation is confined to tiny synthetic linear problems (n=200, d=5 or d=10, T=5,000-20,000 steps). The experiments corroborate the theorems but do not test the practical relevance of the predicted batch-momentum tradeoff in realistic deep-learning settings, which weakens the significance of the practical claims made in the introduction.

Part of the technical foundation (Lemmas C.1-C.8) is restated from Fan et al. (2025), so the genuinely new content is the stochastic/momentum/VR machinery; the contribution is substantial but incremental relative to that full-batch analysis, and the batch-size-one negative result is closely aligned with the per-sample Adam observations of Back et al. (2025).

The variance-reduction result comes with notably worse batch-dependent factors (m^{2+a}) and the paper does not analyze whether practical variants (e.g., partial snapshot updates) could close this rate gap, leaving the VR tradeoff somewhat pessimistic.

Some presentation issues: several results are stated with heavy Big-O expressions whose constant dependencies (e.g., on n, m, beta_1) are hard to parse; the necessity of the large-batch/positive-effective-margin conditions (rather than an artifact of the proof technique) is not established, e.g., no lower bound showing a genuine batch-dependent margin gap.

strengths: Unified framework: The paper analyzes stochastic steepest descent under a common norm-induced geometry covering Normalized-SGD, SignSGD/Signum, Spectral-SGD, and Muon, which makes the results broadly relevant beyond a single optimizer. The random-reshuffling setting is closer to practice than the fixed mini-batch cycling used in prior work (e.g., Baek et al. 2025).

Technically substantive results: The paper provides fully explicit, dimension-free margin convergence rates (Corollaries 4.3, 4.6, 4.8) that strictly improve the dimension-dependent bounds of Fan et al. 2025 (e.g., O((log t+n)/t^{1/2}) vs. O((d log t+nd)/t^{1/2}) at a = 1/2). The mechanism behind the improvement (global ℓ1 control of gradient differences instead of entry-wise bounds) is clearly explained.

Genuinely novel findings: The negative result that without momentum, the large-batch condition necessarily collapses to full batch (Theorem 4.1) plus the clean m = 2 counterexample (Proposition 4.2, with a complete proof showing margins are exactly negated) is a sharp and illuminating characterization. The batch–momentum trade-off (Theorem 4.4: b = Ω(n((1−β1)R/γ)^{1/3})) and the variance-reduction recovery of the exact full-batch bias (Theorem 4.7) are new to the implicit-bias literature.

Careful supporting theory: The technical lemmas (gradient noise bounds under reshuffling, epoch-wise zero-sum cancellation Lemma C.12, explicit t0/c2 constants in Lemma C.15) are worked out in detail, and the extension to exponential loss (Appendix I) shows the framework is not CE-loss-specific.

Honest limitations: The conclusions explicitly acknowledge the linear-model restriction, the gap in the no-momentum regime, and the constructed-dataset nature of the batch-size-one analysis. Experiments (synthetic ℓ2/ℓ∞/spectral, per-sample validation, MNIST two-layer net) qualitatively match all four theoretical regimes.
weaknesses: Scope of the theory: All main results apply only to linear multi-class classifiers on separable data. Given that the motivation is Muon/Adam in LLM pretraining, the connection to the actual algorithms of interest is indirect; the paper itself concedes results 'do not extend directly to nonlinear models.'

The headline no-momentum theorem is largely a full-batch restatement: Theorem 4.1's condition forces b = n, so the positive guarantee is just a (sharper) rederivation of Fan et al. 2025 plus the counterexample. The per-sample result (Theorem 4.10) relies on a highly special orthogonal scale-skewed dataset, so it demonstrates a separation but provides little general characterization of the b = 1 bias.

Conservative and n-dependent rates: The convergence rates contain O(n) 'entry cost' factors and large batch/momentum-dependent constants (m^{2+a}, m/(1−β1)); the practical meaningfulness of the stated rates is unclear, and the momentum analysis does not recover the no-momentum case (Remark 4.5), leaving an unexplained gap between the two regimes.

Assumption 3.4 is nonstandard and tailored: the learning-rate condition on ∑β^s(e^{c1∑η−1}−1) ≤ c2ηt is crafted for the analysis and holds essentially only for polynomial schedules (Lemma C.15); constant step sizes, which dominate practice, are out of scope.

Experimental evidence is modest: only a 200-sample synthetic problem and a 1000-sample MNIST subset with a small two-layer network; the MNIST section (Sec. 5, K.1) is thin, with no code or hyperparameter detail sufficient for full reproducibility of the reported figures.

Presentation issues: several typos and loose statements (e.g., 'In this subsection, We establish', duplicated Assumption 3.2 citation in Lemma F.2, undefined ε in Theorem H.3's proof sketch), and a dense appendix (~55 pages) whose main-line results in Sec. 4 are stated with heavy O(·) expressions that are hard to parse at first read.

strengths: The paper provides the first unified implicit-bias analysis of mini-batch stochastic steepest descent (covering Normalized-SGD, SignSGD/Signum, and Spectral-SGD/Muon) under random reshuffling, with explicit margin-gap bounds and convergence rates (Theorems 4.1, 4.4, 4.7).

The counterexample in Proposition 4.2 (failure of random-reshuffling SignSGD at m = 2 with n = 2) is clean, exact, and convincingly shows that the full-batch-only guarantee in Theorem 4.1 is not merely an artifact of a loose large-batch condition.

The technical machinery in Appendix C (e.g., Lemma C.12 exploiting the epoch-wise zero-sum structure of reshuffling under momentum, Lemma C.15 giving explicit closed-form constants for Assumption 3.4) is careful and, in places, a genuine improvement over prior work — e.g., removing the dimension-d dependence present in Fan et al. [2025].

The variance-reduction result (Theorem 4.7) — recovering the exact full-batch norm-induced max margin for any batch size — is a new and interesting observation about how SVRG-style estimators affect implicit bias, complementing known acceleration results.

Experiments (synthetic multi-class, per-sample validation in Appendix J, MNIST two-layer network) are consistent with the theory, and the limitations section is honest and accurate about the linear-separable scope.
weaknesses: Mismatch between motivation and results: the paper motivates the work via LLM pretraining, Adam, and Muon, but all positive results concern linear classifiers on linearly separable data with decaying learning rates. The practical reach of the theory is narrow, and the batch-size-one analysis (Theorem 4.10) relies on a specially constructed orthogonal scale-skewed dataset, limiting the generality of the 'fundamentally different bias' claim.

The headline no-momentum theorem (Theorem 4.1) is largely a negative result: the large-batch condition collapses to b = n, so the 'convergence guarantee' reduces to the already-known full-batch case (Corollary 4.3 is essentially restated from Fan et al. [2025]). The paper's main positive content is therefore concentrated in the momentum and VR sections, whose constants are very conservative (e.g., the batch requirement b = Ω(n((1−β1)R/γ)^{1/3}) only permits b = Ω(1) when 1 − β1 = O(n^{−3}); margin-gap bounds involve hidden threshold times t2 and factors scaling with m³/(1−β1)).

Rates are worst-case upper bounds only, with no lower bounds or tightness results; the claimed batch–momentum trade-off (γ − ρ vanishing as b↑ or β1→1) follows from a crude sufficient condition, and it is unclear the dependence on m and (1−β1) is meaningful rather than proof-artifact.

Heavy reliance on prior work: the proxy-function framework, many core lemmas (C.1–C.8), and the overall proof architecture are directly adapted from Fan et al. [2025], and the per-sample departure phenomenon closely mirrors Baek et al. [2025]; the genuinely new technical content is the stochastic noise handling under reshuffling, which is a solid but incremental advance.

Several parts of the appendix proofs are informal or sketchy ('we just follow the same steps in Lemma D.1, E.1'), Assumption 3.4 is a nonstandard and opaque condition whose satisfaction is only verified post hoc for polynomial schedules, and the manuscript contains numerous typos and presentation errors (e.g., 'sequnece', 'Fisrt', 'similat', inconsistent notation for norms) that reduce polish.

Experimental evidence is limited to small linear/synthetic problems and one small MNIST setup; no experiments probe whether the predicted batch–momentum thresholds (t2 scaling, ρ > 0 conditions) are quantitatively predictive.

strengths: The paper provides a unified framework for the implicit bias of stochastic steepest descent under general entry-wise and Schatten-p norm geometries, covering SignSGD/Signum, Normalized-SGD, Spectral-SGD/Muon and their momentum and variance-reduced variants. This breadth (batch size, momentum, variance reduction) is more systematic than prior analyses, which were limited to full-batch steepest descent (Fan et al., 2025) or proxy algorithms like per-sample Adam (Baek et al., 2025).

The negative result for momentum-free updates is well supported: the large-batch condition is shown to collapse to the full-batch regime under the stated assumptions, and Proposition 4.2 gives a clean, concrete counterexample (n=2, m=2) showing failure is not merely due to looseness of the analysis. This sharpens the message beyond a purely technical artifact.

The momentum analysis (Theorem 4.4) reveals a genuine and interpretable batch-momentum trade-off (effective margin gap vanishing as batch size grows or beta_1 -> 1), and the proofs exploit the epoch-wise zero-sum structure of random reshuffling (Lemma C.12), which is a nice technical observation.

The claimed dimension-free improvement over Fan et al. [2025] is explained concretely (bounding ||grad L(W1) - grad L(W2)||_1 globally rather than entry-wise), and the technical lemmas (e.g., Lemma C.15 giving explicit closed-form t0 and c2 for Assumption 3.4) suggest careful, self-contained derivations with detailed appendices.

The variance-reduction result (Theorem 4.7) that SVRG-style estimators recover the exact full-batch implicit bias for any batch size, at the cost of slower rates, is a novel and practically relevant finding, and the batch-size-one analysis (Theorem 4.10) with an explicit, different limiting direction nicely complements the positive results.

Experiments on synthetic and MNIST data qualitatively match all four theoretical regimes (no momentum, momentum, variance reduction, per-sample), and the limitations section is honest and specific about scope (linear classifiers, separable data, constructed dataset for b=1).
weaknesses: The first main theorem (Theorem 4.1) is nearly vacuous: under the stated assumptions the large-batch condition forces m=1 (full batch), so the 'result' amounts to recovering the known full-batch analysis of Fan et al. [2025] for stochastic steepest descent. The counterexample partially rescues its value, but the contribution of Section 4.1 on its own is limited.

The positive guarantees for momentum are approximate (convergence to margin rho < gamma, not the max-margin solution) and the required condition b = Omega(n((1-beta1)R/gamma)^{1/3}) may not be tight; there are no lower bounds matching the 1/3 exponent or the m/(1-beta1) rate factors, so the sharpness of the batch-momentum trade-off claimed in the abstract is not fully established.

The analysis is confined to linear multi-class classifiers on linearly separable data with strongly polynomial learning rates (eta_t = t^{-a}, a <= 1); this excludes constant step sizes and practical schedules, and does not directly speak to deep or even homogeneous nonlinear models, which limits practical reach despite the Muon/AdamW motivation.

Several technical assumptions are non-standard or heavy: Assumption 3.4 is an intricate condition on the learning-rate schedule needed for momentum; Remark 4.5 acknowledges the momentum analysis does not recover the no-momentum case at beta1 = 0, indicating the three analyses (no momentum / momentum / VR) are patched together rather than arising from one truly unified mechanism.

The experiments are small in scale (n=200 synthetic, 1000 MNIST samples, 20k iterations) and largely confirm already-stated qualitative behavior; there is no code release statement and no quantitative verification of the predicted rate dependencies (e.g., scaling of the gap with m and 1/(1-beta1)), which limits how strongly the theory's quantitative claims are validated.

A substantial part of the technical machinery (proxy function, many lemmas) is adapted from Fan et al. [2025], so the main technical novelty rests on the stochastic-noise lemmas (C.11-C.14) and the batch-momentum interplay; the originality is real but incremental relative to the closest prior work.

Minor presentation issues: typos and small inconsistencies ('perform deeper explorations', 'similat', inconsistent constants such as 4Rn/(gamma+4R) vs 4Rn/(gamma+R)), and the variance-reduction constant scaling (m^{2+a} vs m^3 depending on a) makes the rate statements hard to parse across corollaries.
